ety.text: From Middle English puff, puf, from Old English pyf (“a blast of wind, puff”), from Proto-West Germanic *puf(f)- (“to blow, puff”), of imitative origin. Cognate with Dutch puf (“puff, wind, fart”), Middle Low German puf, pof (“puff”).

chain.g: to breathe out, blow with the mouth

ety.text: From Middle English puffen, from Old English pyffan (“to breathe out, blow with the mouth”). Compare Dutch puffen, German Low German puffen, German puffen, Danish puffe, Swedish puffa.

senses.d: A sharp exhalation of a small amount of breath through the mouth.
The ability to breathe easily while exerting oneself.
ex: out of puff

senses.d: A small quantity of gas or smoke in the air.
ex: puff of smoke

senses.d: A sudden but small gust of wind, smoke, etc.
ex: to every puff of wind a slave
"The wind we had was only an early puff! You'll see we shall have our full allowance!"

senses.d: An act of inhaling smoke from a cigarette, cigar or pipe.
The drug cannabis.
A flamboyant or alluring statement of praise.
ex: […] though I care not one straw for the personal puffs of which I myself am so often the subject […]
[…] we critics were not his fellow-guests, but simply deadheads whose business it was to "dress the house" and write puffs.

senses.d: A portion of fabric gathered up so as to be left full in the middle.
ex: a sleeve with a puff at the shoulder

senses.d: A light cake filled with cream, cream cheese, etc.
ex: cream puff

senses.d: A puffball.
ex: Bozzacchio, an acorne. Also a puffe or mushrump full of dust.

senses.d: To emit smoke, gas, etc., in puffs.
ex: Still on the down line, the engine puffed away to the South, and in a few moments had disappeared in the darkness!

senses.d: To pant.
ex: By and by comes the ass back again, Puffing and Blowing, from the Chase.
Puffing and panting, we plodded on until within about a mile of the harbor we came upon a sight that brought us all up standing.

senses.d: To advertise.
To blow as an expression of scorn.
ex: It is really to defy Heaven to puff at damnation.

senses.d: To swell with air; to be dilated or inflated.
ex: 'tis easy for a man to have a great opinion of his own knowledge , and be puff'd up by it

senses.d: To breathe in a swelling, inflated, or pompous manner; hence, to assume importance.
ex: Then came brave Glory puffing by.

senses.d: To drive with a puff, or with puffs.
ex: The clearing north will puff the clouds away.

senses.d: To repel with words; to blow at contemptuously.
ex: I puff the prostitute away.

senses.d: To cause to swell or dilate; to inflate.
ex: a bladder puffed with air
the sea puffed up with winds

senses.d: To inflate with pride, flattery, self-esteem, etc.; often with up.
ex: puffed up with military success

grp.label: sharp exhalation of a small amount of breath through the mouth
ability to breathe easily while exerting oneself
small quantity of gas or smoke in the air
informal: act of inhaling smoke from a cigarette, cigar or pipe

fr:souffle.gl: blowing (act of expelling air from the mouth)

chain.g: to blow, to puff up, to inflate

ety.text: Inherited from Latin flātus. Doublet of flato.
Deverbal from soffiare + -o. Compare Sicilian çuççu.
From bocca (“mouth”) + -ata. Compare Vulgar Latin *buccata, French bouchée, Romanian bucată, Portuguese bocado, and Spanish bocado.

pt:pitada.gl: pinch (a small amount of a powder-like substance)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese erva, from Latin herba, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”). Cognate with Galician herba and Spanish hierba.
From Kimbundu makanha, plural of rikanha (“tobacco”).
